title: Functional & Logic Languages
summary: Haskell, OCaml, F#, Elixir, Erlang, Clojure and Prolog: languages that treat programs as expressions, messages or logic. Monads are the threshold: a way to sequence effects in a pure language, and a pattern you already use as promises and optionals.
sources: Lipovača: Learn You a Haskell for Great Good!
Minsky, Madhavapeddy, Hickey: Real World OCaml
Sterling & Shapiro: The Art of Prolog

nodes.label: Haskell: Purity & Laziness
nodes.summary: Pure functions and lazy evaluation: nothing runs until its value is needed.
nodes.outcome: Use an infinite list safely because of laziness.
nodes.check: In Haskell, when is an expression evaluated?
nodes.answer: Only when its value is needed (lazy evaluation).

nodes.label: Type Inference
nodes.summary: Hindley–Milner inference: strong static types with few annotations.
nodes.outcome: Read an inferred type signature and explain it.
nodes.check: In OCaml or Haskell, must you annotate the type of every function?
nodes.answer: No: the compiler infers most types automatically.

nodes.label: Algebraic Data Types & Pattern Matching
nodes.summary: Sum and product types, with the compiler checking that every case is handled.
nodes.outcome: Model a domain with sum types and exhaustive matches.
nodes.check: What does the compiler check when you pattern-match on a sum type such as Maybe or Option?

nodes.label: Monads: Sequencing Effects
nodes.summary: A uniform way to chain computations that carry context: failure, state, I/O, async. Troublesome because the abstraction is taught before the examples.
nodes.outcome: Chain Maybe and IO computations with do-notation.
nodes.check: Why does Haskell need something like the IO monad at all?
nodes.answer: Functions are pure, so effects like I/O are represented as values that are sequenced explicitly.

nodes.label: "Monads are a Haskell curiosity"
nodes.summary: Promises, async/await, optional chaining and list comprehensions follow the same pattern.
nodes.outcome: Recognise monadic patterns in mainstream code.
nodes.check: Name a monad-like pattern you can use in mainstream languages.
nodes.answer: Promises and async/await, Optional or Maybe chaining, or list comprehensions.

nodes.label: The Actor Model
nodes.summary: Isolated processes that share nothing and communicate by messages.
nodes.outcome: Design a system of communicating processes.
nodes.check: How do Erlang and Elixir processes share data?
nodes.answer: They don't share memory; they send each other messages.

nodes.label: Elixir & Erlang: Let It Crash
nodes.summary: Lightweight processes and supervisors on the BEAM, built for telecom-grade uptime.
nodes.outcome: Build a supervision tree that restarts failed workers.
nodes.check: What does 'let it crash' mean on the BEAM?
nodes.answer: Processes don't defensively handle every error; supervisors restart failed processes in a known good state.

nodes.label: Lisp & Clojure: Code as Data
nodes.summary: Programs written as lists, so code can be generated and transformed with macros.
nodes.outcome: Write a small macro in Clojure or Scheme.
nodes.answer: Code is written in the language's own data structures (lists), so programs can manipulate code with macros.

nodes.label: "Recursion is always slower than loops"
nodes.summary: Tail calls can reuse the current stack frame, so tail recursion runs like a loop.
nodes.outcome: Rewrite a recursive function in tail-recursive form.
nodes.check: Why doesn't a tail-recursive function grow the stack in Haskell, OCaml or Scheme?
nodes.answer: Tail-call optimisation reuses the current frame, so it runs like a loop.

nodes.label: OCaml & F#: Functional in Industry
nodes.summary: Pragmatic ML-family languages used in finance, compilers and .NET shops.
nodes.outcome: Write a small parser in OCaml or F#.
nodes.check: Which platform does F# run on?

nodes.label: Prolog: Logic Programming
nodes.summary: Facts, rules and queries; the engine searches for answers by unification and backtracking.
nodes.outcome: Write a family-tree program and query it.
nodes.check: In Prolog, what do you write instead of step-by-step instructions?
nodes.answer: Facts and rules; the system searches for answers to queries.
